scenes.heading: Intermolecular forces
scenes.sub: Why is water a liquid but methane a gas?
scenes.say: Covalent bonds hold atoms together inside a molecule. But what holds molecules close to each other? Without these forces, every molecular substance would be a gas.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Friend groups hold hands tightly but drift apart at the bell
scenes.science: Boiling breaks forces between molecules, not bonds inside them
scenes.breaks: the hand-holding is really shared electrons, and the pull between groups is attraction between partial charges.
scenes.say: Picture friend groups at a school assembly, each holding hands tightly. Each group is a molecule, and the hand-holding is the strong covalent bonds. Groups are loosely drawn to each other, like weak intermolecular forces. When the bell rings, the groups drift apart, but nobody lets go. That's boiling: steam is still H two O.
scenes.caption: Picture friend groups at a school assembly, each holding hands tightly. Each group is a molecule, and the hand-holding is the strong covalent bonds. Groups are loosely drawn to each other, like weak intermolecular forces. When the bell rings, the groups drift apart, but nobody lets go. That's boiling: steam is still H₂O.

scenes.heading: Dispersion forces
scenes.say: Dispersion forces act between all molecules. Moving electrons create temporary dipoles that attract neighbours. More electrons means stronger forces. And long, straight molecules touch more, like spaghetti, so they stick better than compact meatballs.

scenes.heading: Dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonds
points: Polar molecules: δ+ end attracts δ− end
Hydrogen bond: H bonded to F, O or N
...attracted to a lone pair on F, O or N
scenes.say: Polar molecules also have dipole–dipole attractions: the slightly positive end of one attracts the slightly negative end of another. Hydrogen bonding is an extra-strong version. Remember FON: hydrogen must be bonded to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, and attracted to a lone pair on one of those.

scenes.heading: The burger checklist
steps: Cheese: H on F, O or N? add H-bonds
scenes.say: Use the burger checklist. Every molecule gets the bun: dispersion forces. Add the patty if it's polar: dipole–dipole. Add the cheese only if it has hydrogen on F, O or N: hydrogen bonding. Stronger forces overall means a higher boiling point.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Which intermolecular forces act between methanol (CH₃OH) molecules?
lines: C–O and O–H bonds make it polar: dipole–dipole
Has an O–H bond: hydrogen bonding
scenes.say: What forces act between methanol molecules? Every molecule has dispersion forces. Its C O and O H bonds make it polar, so add dipole–dipole. And it has an O H bond, so add hydrogen bonding. Methanol has all three.
scenes.caption: What forces act between methanol molecules? Every molecule has dispersion forces. Its C–O and O–H bonds make it polar, so add dipole–dipole. And it has an O–H bond, so add hydrogen bonding. Methanol has all three.

scenes.heading: Water is special
points: High boiling point for its size
Ice is an open cage, so it floats
scenes.say: Hydrogen bonding makes water special. It gives water a high boiling point for its size and a high heat capacity. In ice, hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open cage, so ice is less dense than water and floats.

points: Dispersion: all molecules, more e⁻ = stronger
Hydrogen bonding: H on F, O or N
scenes.say: Quick recap. Boiling only breaks the forces between molecules. Dispersion forces act everywhere and grow with more electrons. Polar molecules add dipole–dipole. Hydrogen bonding needs H on F, O or N. Now try the practice questions!
